script: Anyone who has moved house in this province in the last decade will have met the tenancy deposit scheme, and most people encounter it twice, initially on payment and subsequently when attempting recovery. The scheme was introduced because deposits were being withheld for reasons that were never written down, and it works by taking the money out of the landlord's hands entirely. Within fifteen days of receiving a deposit, a landlord must lodge it with one of three approved bodies and give the tenant a certificate showing where it sits. The tenant has no obligation at that stage although the certificate merits retention because it initiates any subsequent dispute procedure. At the conclusion of the tenancy the landlord proposes any deduction and the tenant either agrees or disputes it. If both agree, the money is released within ten working days, and the scheme takes no view on whether the deduction was reasonable in the first place. If they do not, either side may refer the matter to the scheme's adjudicator, whose decision binds both and costs nothing to either. The adjudicator sees only documents: the inventory taken at the start, photographs, receipts for any work claimed. This is where most disputes are actually decided, which explains why every tenancy service offers identical unglamorous advice about photographing the property on arrival and again on departure. A landlord who has not lodged the deposit at all faces a separate penalty of up to three times its value, and the tenant may claim it whether or not there is any dispute about the state of the property.

items.stem: What must a landlord do within fifteen days?
options: Lodge the deposit and issue a certificate
Return the deposit to the tenant
Complete a full inventory of the property
Register the tenancy with the local council
items.rationale: The passage states the deposit must be lodged with an approved body and a certificate given to the tenant within fifteen days.

items.stem: Why is the certificate worth keeping?
options: It starts the later dispute process
It proves the rent has been paid
It is demanded by the council
items.rationale: The text says the tenant need do nothing at that stage but the certificate is the document that starts the dispute process later.

items.stem: What does the adjudicator base a decision on?
items.rationale: The adjudicator sees only documents: the inventory, photographs and receipts for work claimed.

items.stem: Why is the standard advice about photographs given?
items.rationale: The passage links the dull advice directly to the fact that most disputes are decided on documents.

items.stem: What happens if a deposit was never lodged?
options: A penalty of up to triple the sum
The deposit is returned at once
The landlord may no longer deduct
items.rationale: The final sentence describes a separate penalty of up to three times the deposit, claimable regardless of any dispute.

script: The staff development fund exists to pay for training that the department could not otherwise afford, and the rules around it are more particular than most people realise. Any employee past their probation may apply, and applications are considered four times a year rather than as they arrive, which is the first thing that catches people out: a course starting in three weeks will almost certainly not be funded, because the panel that approves the money will not have met. The fund pays course fees in full and travel at the standard rate. It does not pay for equipment, for professional membership, or for the time spent studying, and a manager who has agreed to release someone for two days a month has agreed to something the fund plays no part in. Applications are ranked, not simply approved or refused, and the ranking is against the department's published skills gaps rather than against the applicant's own plans. This produces the outcome staff find hardest to accept: a well-argued application for a qualification the department does not currently need will lose to a modest one that closes a named gap. Where an application is refused, the panel gives its reason in writing, and an applicant who reapplies at the next round having addressed it is markedly more likely to succeed. Last year, eleven of the fourteen successful second applications had been refused once. Applicants are also asked to say what will change in their work as a result of the course, and the panel treats a vague answer here as a weak application however strong the rest of it reads. The fund is not, and has never been, first come first served.

items.stem: Why might a course starting soon not be funded?
options: The panel meets only four times a year
The fund is usually exhausted by then
Fees rise close to the start date
items.rationale: Applications are considered four times a year, so a course starting in three weeks falls before the panel has met.

items.stem: What does the fund NOT cover?
items.rationale: The passage lists equipment, professional membership and study time as things the fund does not pay for.

items.stem: What are applications ranked against?
options: The total cost of the course
items.rationale: The ranking is explicitly against the department's published skills gaps rather than the applicant's own plans.

items.stem: Why do staff find the ranking hard to accept?
options: A strong case can lose to a modest one
Written reasons are only rarely provided
The membership of the panel is confidential
The published skills gaps change every year
items.rationale: A well-argued application for an unneeded qualification loses to a modest one that closes a named gap.

items.stem: What does the figure of eleven out of fourteen show?
options: Reapplying after a refusal often works
The panel rarely changes its mind
items.rationale: Eleven of fourteen successful second applications had been refused once, supporting the claim that addressing the written reason helps.

script: Community allotments in this city are administered by the parks department, and demand has run ahead of supply for so long that the waiting list has become the main thing the department manages. There are 1,900 plots and roughly 4,400 people waiting, and the average wait is now a little over five years, though that figure conceals a wide range. Two sites in the north have plots free most summers, while the two nearest the university have not released one in eighteen months. Applicants may join one list only, which is checked against the electoral roll, and moving house within the city does not lose your place. What does lose it is a missed offer. A plot is offered by letter and by email, and an applicant who does not reply within twenty-eight days is returned to the bottom rather than the middle. The department describes that rule as harsh and defends it as necessary. Before it was introduced, plots stood empty for a season while offers passed down a list of people who had lost interest years earlier. Plot holders pay an annual rent scaled to plot size, with a reduction for those over sixty-five and for anyone receiving certain benefits. Cultivation is inspected twice a year, and a plot found substantially uncultivated on both visits is reclaimed after a written warning and a second inspection. The department stresses that the standard is cultivation and not tidiness. A plot deliberately left rough for wildlife is not at risk if it is recorded with the site secretary.

items.stem: What does the five-year average conceal?
options: The true number of plots free
The cost of renting a plot
items.rationale: The passage says the figure hides a wide range, with northern sites free most summers and university sites releasing nothing for eighteen months.

items.stem: What causes an applicant to lose their place?
options: Not replying to an offer in time
items.rationale: An applicant who does not reply within twenty-eight days goes to the bottom of the list; moving within the city does not lose a place.

items.stem: How does the department defend that rule?
options: Plots once stood empty for a season
It is required by the council
items.rationale: Before the rule, offers passed down a list of people who had lost interest and plots stood empty for a season.

items.stem: When is a plot reclaimed?
options: After two failed inspections and a warning
As soon as rent goes unpaid
When the holder leaves the city
items.rationale: A plot substantially uncultivated on both visits is reclaimed after a written warning and a second inspection.

items.stem: What is the inspection standard?
items.rationale: The department stresses cultivation, not tidiness, and exempts a plot left rough for wildlife if recorded with the site secretary.

script: Volunteer drivers take patients to hospital appointments that public transport cannot reach in time, and the scheme is older than most of the services it supports. Drivers use their own cars and are reimbursed per kilometre at a rate set annually. The rate is not a payment and is deliberately set below the level at which it would become taxable income, which is the reason it has not risen with fuel prices. Every driver is checked before their first journey and re-checked every three years. They must carry business-use insurance, which many insurers add without charge once the purpose is explained, though a minority treat it as a change of use and increase the premium. The coordinator keeps a list of which insurers do what, and it is worth asking before renewing rather than after. Drivers choose their own journeys from a weekly list and are asked, though not required, to take at least two a month, since the scheme's reliability rests on regularity rather than on numbers. A driver may not accept money, gifts or shopping requests from a patient, and this rule causes more difficulty than any other, because patients are grateful and offering something is how gratitude is normally expressed. The coordinator's advice is to name the rule rather than refuse the gift, which moves the refusal from the driver to the scheme. Journeys involving stretchers, oxygen or a patient who cannot be left alone are not part of the scheme and are booked through the ambulance service instead.

items.stem: Why has the reimbursement rate not risen with fuel prices?
options: A higher rate would become taxable
The scheme has no budget for it
No driver has ever requested it
items.rationale: The rate is deliberately set below the level at which it would become taxable income, which is given as the reason.

items.stem: What does the passage say about insurers?
options: Practice varies, so ask before renewing
All of them charge an extra premium
None of them charge an extra premium
items.rationale: Many add business use without charge, a minority raise the premium, and the coordinator keeps a list worth consulting before renewal.

items.stem: Why are drivers asked to take two journeys a month?
options: The weekly list is otherwise too long
It keeps their background check valid
It qualifies them for the rate
items.rationale: The passage says the scheme's reliability rests on regularity rather than numbers.

items.stem: Which rule is described as the hardest in practice?
options: Choosing journeys from a weekly list
items.rationale: The ban on money, gifts and shopping requests is said to cause more difficulty than any other, because offering something is how gratitude is expressed.

items.stem: What is the coordinator's advice about gifts?
items.rationale: Naming the rule moves the refusal from the driver to the scheme, which is the advice given.

script: There is a proposal before the council to make the city's buses free at the point of use, and it is being argued almost entirely on the wrong ground. Supporters point to the fare revenue, which covers thirty-one per cent of operating cost, and present the remaining sixty-nine as evidence that the fare is nearly symbolic already. Opponents point to the same thirty-one and call it a hole that would have to be filled from somewhere. Both are treating the fare as a financial instrument, and it is not primarily that. A fare is a rationing device, and the question that decides whether removing it is wise is whether this network has spare capacity to ration. On six of our eleven routes it plainly does: buses run at under forty per cent of seated capacity outside the two peaks, and additional passengers on those services cost almost nothing to carry. On the other five, and on all eleven between half past seven and nine, the buses are already full, and a free service would not add riders so much as redistribute the misery. A passenger who now waits for the second bus would wait for the third. The experience of cities that have done this is consistent on exactly this point. Ridership rises between twenty and sixty per cent, the rise is concentrated where there was room, and where there was not, the reliability figures fall within a year and the political case collapses with them. None of this is an argument against free buses. It is an argument that the sequence matters more than the decision: capacity first, then the fare. A council that reverses the order will spend the money, lose the reliability, and be told by its own voters that the experiment failed, when what failed was the ordering.

items.stem: What does the writer say both sides get wrong?
options: They treat the fare as only financial
They quote the revenue figure wrongly
They ignore the cost of new buses
They rely on other cities' figures
items.rationale: Both sides argue from the thirty-one per cent, and the writer says a fare is primarily a rationing device rather than a financial instrument.

items.stem: What decides whether removing the fare is wise?
options: Whether the subsidy can be found
items.rationale: The writer states the deciding question is whether the network has spare capacity to ration.

items.stem: What happens on the busiest services?
options: Fares rise to compensate for it
Extra buses are put on quickly
items.rationale: On full routes a free service would redistribute the misery: a passenger who waits for the second bus would wait for the third.

items.stem: What do other cities' results show, on this account?
options: Gains occur where there was room
Operating costs fall within a year
items.rationale: Ridership rises by twenty to sixty per cent, concentrated where there was room, with reliability falling where there was not.

items.stem: What is the writer's actual conclusion?
options: Capacity should come before the fare
Free buses should be rejected outright
The fare should be raised instead
The council should consult its voters
items.rationale: The writer says this is not an argument against free buses but that the sequence matters: capacity first, then the fare.

script: Whenever a public body is criticised for slowness, the reform that follows is a target, and the target is almost always a time. Answer within ten days. Assess within four weeks. The appeal of a time target is that it is unambiguous and can be published, and both of those are genuine virtues in a body that has previously published nothing. What is less often noticed is that a time target is a claim about the distribution of work as well as the speed of it, and that the claim is usually false. Cases do not arrive in a uniform stream of comparable difficulty. They arrive in a long tail, in which most are quick and a small minority are genuinely hard. A target applied to the average is met by doing the quick ones faster, which is worth something. A target applied to every case is met by doing the hard ones badly, or by reclassifying them until they are no longer the kind of case the target covers, and the second is far more common than the first, because it requires no one to do anything visibly wrong. I have watched three organisations adopt near-identical targets. In each, the published figure improved, and in each, the number of cases recorded as complex, and therefore exempt, roughly doubled within two years. The people running these bodies were not cynical. They were responding to the only instrument they had been given. If a target must be set, it should be set on the tail, at the ninetieth percentile, published alongside the count of cases excluded from it. That is the number that cannot be improved by moving work between categories, and it is also the number that describes what a person unlucky enough to have a difficult case will actually experience.

items.stem: What false claim does a time target make?
options: That cases are of comparable difficulty
That the staff are working too slowly
That appeals against decisions are rare
items.rationale: The writer argues a time target is a claim about the distribution of work, and cases arrive in a long tail rather than uniformly.

items.stem: How is a universal target usually met?
options: By refusing to take new cases
items.rationale: It is met by doing hard cases badly or, far more commonly, by reclassifying them out of the target's scope.

items.stem: What did the writer observe in three organisations?
options: Staff numbers fell year on year
items.rationale: In each, the published figure improved while the number of cases recorded as complex, and therefore exempt, roughly doubled.

items.stem: How does the writer characterise the managers involved?
options: Indifferent to the public they serve
items.rationale: The passage says they were not cynical but were responding to the only instrument they had been given.

items.stem: What does the writer propose?
options: A target applied to the average only
Targets set by an outside regulator
items.rationale: The conclusion recommends setting the target on the tail, published alongside the count of excluded cases.

script: The case for teaching handwriting in an age of keyboards is usually made badly, and the bad version deserves the impatience it receives. It says that handwriting is a discipline, that it builds character, and that something is lost when a child no longer forms letters by hand, claims which may all be true and none of which can be tested. The better case is narrower and rests on findings that are not in serious dispute. Writing by hand is slower than typing for almost everyone past the first year of practice, and in note-taking that slowness is not a defect but the mechanism: a student who cannot record everything must decide what matters, and deciding what matters is most of what learning a lecture consists of. Students who type produce fuller, more verbatim notes and perform worse on questions that require them to draw a conclusion, while performing about the same on questions of simple recall. That pattern has held across a number of replications, including several that failed to reproduce other effects claimed in the same literature. It says nothing whatever about character, and nothing about whether children should learn cursive, which is a separate question about a particular form. What it supports is a modest and rather boring proposition: that the speed of a recording tool changes what is recorded, that slower tools force selection, and that selection is where the understanding happens. It is also a proposition with a limit worth stating: it concerns note-taking under time pressure, and says nothing about a student reading at their own pace, where no selection is forced and the tool matters much less. Anyone who wants to defend handwriting should defend that, and should stop defending the other thing, which is untestable and which makes the testable claim look like part of the same argument.

items.stem: What does the writer say about the usual case?
options: It overstates the role of speed
items.rationale: The usual case appeals to discipline and character, claims the writer says may be true but cannot be tested.

items.stem: Why is slowness described as the mechanism?
options: It forces the writer to select
It improves the quality of writing
It leaves more time for revision
items.rationale: A student who cannot record everything must decide what matters, and that deciding is most of what learning a lecture consists of.

items.stem: What pattern do the findings show?
options: Typists do worse on inference only
Typists do worse on every measure
items.rationale: Typists produce fuller notes and do worse on questions requiring a conclusion while performing about the same on simple recall.

items.stem: Why does the writer mention replications?
options: The effect survived where others did not
items.rationale: The pattern held across replications, including ones that failed to reproduce other effects in the same literature.

items.stem: What does the writer advise defenders to do?
items.rationale: The closing argument is to defend the modest testable proposition and stop defending the untestable one, which contaminates it.

script: Our professional body is consulting on whether to require thirty hours of continuing education a year, up from twenty, and the consultation asks the wrong question. It asks whether thirty hours is the right number. The right question is whether hours are the right unit, and the answer has been available for some time. Hours measure attendance. They do not measure whether anything was learned, and the two come apart in a way that is easy to observe: the members who most need updating are precisely the ones who satisfy an hours requirement most cheaply, by sitting through whatever is nearest and cheapest, while the members who least need it choose demanding courses and would have done so with no requirement at all. Raising the number does not close that gap. It widens it, because the cheapest way to find ten more hours is worse than the cheapest way to find the first twenty. I would not abolish the requirement. A floor has value even when it measures the wrong thing, because it removes the option of doing nothing at all, and the profession has members who would take it. The consultation document itself concedes, in a single line near the end, that it holds no evidence that the current twenty hours has changed anyone's practice, and that concession is more interesting than the question it is attached to. But the increase should be spent differently. Ten hours of the thirty could be required to produce something a colleague reads: a case note, a short protocol, a teaching session delivered to one's own department. That is measurable in a way attendance is not, because either the thing exists or it does not. It also has the property that no one can produce it by sitting at the back of a room, which is the whole of the problem the consultation is trying to solve and the one thing another ten hours cannot touch.

items.stem: What does the writer say the consultation gets wrong?
options: It asks about the number, not the unit
It consults far too few members
It assumes the current rule works
It ignores the cost to members
items.rationale: The consultation asks whether thirty is the right number when the question is whether hours are the right unit.

items.stem: Why does raising the requirement widen the gap?
options: The cheapest extra hours are worse
items.rationale: The writer argues the cheapest way to find ten more hours is worse than the cheapest way to find the first twenty.

items.stem: Why would the writer keep a requirement at all?
options: Inaction would otherwise be an option
It is required by current legislation
Members have come to expect it
items.rationale: A floor has value even measuring the wrong thing because it removes the option of doing nothing, which some members would take.

items.stem: What does the writer propose for ten of the hours?
items.rationale: Ten hours would have to produce a case note, protocol or teaching session — something a colleague reads.

items.stem: What property makes that proposal attractive?
options: It cannot be met by attending
It costs the members far less
It is much easier to administer
items.rationale: No one can produce such a thing by sitting at the back of a room, which is the problem the writer says extra hours cannot touch.
